chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Mahbub from Shihab from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who freed his slave on the evening of 'Arafah, does it count for the slave as the Hajj of Islam? He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'And if the master performs Hajj for an Umm al-Walad (female slave who bears his child), does it count for her?' He said, 'No.' I said, 'Does she have a reward in her own Hajj?' He said, 'Yes.'

key_terms.أُمُّ وَلَدٍ: Umm al-Walad (a female slave who bears a child to her master)
key_terms.حَجَّةَ اَلْإِسْلاَمِ: the Hajj of Islam (the first/fundamental obligatory pilgrimage)

ai.seo_question: Does freeing a slave on the evening of Arafah count as their obligatory Hajj?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the specific conditions under which manumission fulfills the duty of Hajj, noting that freeing a slave on the evening of 'Arafah is sufficient for their obligatory Hajj. However, he distinguishes this from the case of an *Umm al-Walad* (a slave who bears her master's child), where the master's Hajj on her behalf does not discharge her personal obligation, though she still accrues spiritual reward. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on the distinct legal status of *Umm al-Walad* and the necessity of personal performance for her fundamental Hajj duty.
